edus.text: If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had summited Mount Everest in 1924 and survived to return home, the history of mountaineering—and perhaps aspects of British cultural identity—would have shifted dramatically.
First, the summit of Everest would have been achieved nearly three decades earlier than in reality, and without supplemental oxygen technology at a modern level.

Their success would have crowned the British expeditions of the 1920s as the definitive triumph of the so-called “Third Pole” race, embedding Everest firmly in the narrative of late imperial British heroism.
Instead of becoming tragic symbols of noble failure, Mallory and Irvine would have been celebrated as living embodiments of endurance, ingenuity, and imperial resolve.

In the interwar period, when Britain was grappling with the trauma of World War I and signs of imperial decline, their success would likely have been used as a powerful symbol of national resilience and global leadership.
Mountaineering history would also have changed.
A confirmed 1924 ascent would have reoriented debates about high-altitude capability, particularly concerning oxygen use.
If they had succeeded with the relatively primitive oxygen systems of the time, it might have accelerated technical innovation in high-altitude gear and normalized supplemental oxygen earlier.
Conversely, if they had reached the summit with minimal reliance on oxygen, it could have strengthened the ethos of “pure” climbing much earlier in the sport’s development.

The 1953 ascent by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay would not have been framed as the first conquest of Everest, but perhaps as the first ascent by a new route, the first without oxygen (if applicable), or the first fully documented and widely photographed success.
The mythology of Everest would also be different.
In reality, Mallory’s disappearance created one of mountaineering’s great mysteries, fueling decades of speculation and romantic fascination.
If they had returned alive, Everest might have lost some of its aura as an almost supernatural killer peak during the interwar years.
A successful 1924 climb could have encouraged more aggressive expeditions in the 1930s, possibly leading to earlier commercial or national competition on the mountain.
The mountain might have been seen less as an unknowable enigma and more as a formidable but conquerable objective.
On a broader geopolitical level, a British success in 1924 would have preempted later achievements by other nations.
Swiss, German, and eventually New Zealand and Nepali climbers would have entered a field already defined by British primacy.
Given the importance of symbolic “firsts,” Britain would have permanently claimed the ultimate mountaineering milestone.
Finally, Mallory himself would be remembered differently.
Instead of being immortalized for his poetic “Because it’s there,” he might have become a leading voice in mountaineering technique, training, and exploration.
Irvine, young and technically skilled, might have shaped the engineering side of high-altitude equipment.
Their survival would have replaced legend with testimony, mystery with memoir.

In short, if Mallory and Irvine had summited and survived in 1924, Everest would still be formidable—but its story would be less tragic and more triumphant, and the golden age of Himalayan climbing would have begun under the Union Jack nearly thirty years earlier.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. Rating Indicator ​ Rating Description ​ G ​ General Audiences - All Ages Admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children whether viewing together with parents or by themselves. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. R ​ Restricted - Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them with proper legal identification at the box office. NC-17 ​ Adults Only - No One 17 Years And Under Admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not legally admitted and all adults must have legal identification at the box office. With the Film Rating System in place to ensure film producers and film distributors have the creative freedom to pursue the projects they want to make, there could be other ways for the Legion of Decency and various religion and social rights groups could clean up Hollywood for film, radio and eventually television without hampering creative freedom. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. Entertainment, education and information fit for religious viewers. They would take in the various technological and artistic talents and know-how from the secular Hollywood studios and apply them towards delivering motion pictures (narrative feature and even the documentaries) with high production standards and quality to deliver their messages to the masses while showing religion on the side of freedom versus tyranny. This would also filter down to local radio stations (and eventually television stations starting in the late 1940s) that would choose to become affiliates of the religious non-denominational Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) which would be listener and eventually viewer-supported to broadcast religious services, national and international news along with news analysis and commentary, local community sports highlights and commentary, charity events, and even motion pictures from the Holy Light library after they finish their original theatrical runs come the advent of television. Local, state and federal non-partisan movements and educational institutions such as colleges, universities, trade schools and public schools would take advantage of the creative and editorial freedoms to organize radio (and eventually television) stations under one coast-to-coast network to provide listener/viewer-supported entertainment/culture, public affairs, educational and community outreach programming for the masses. National Public Radio (NPR) and the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) would both provide alternatives to the commercial broadcast radio (and eventually television) networks found in the American Broadcasting Company (ABC - formerly NBC Blue), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC - formerly NBC Red). All of them would agree, however, that their news reporting standards were to be "factual, fair and without bias" and any commentary and analysis from a partisan political viewpoint should be "clearly defined as such". While NPR and TBN were listener and eventually viewer-supported from the beginning; ABC, CBS and NBC would ensure that commercial time would be limited during hours when children and teenagers would be most likely to be tuning in. The commercial networks would choose to give fair and equal time, coverage and analysis of viewpoints and educational/informative programs to keep up with NPR and TBN's higher standards. However, there was another effect of the Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio decision - the major movie studios could not buy and own the cinema companies that their films would be released to. This would be an antitrust compromise with the governments so that no corporate body could block the release of a film in a release slot that could pose a risk to another company's releases. What would the ripple effects of all this combined be on the motion picture and radio studios and distributors of the time (20th Century-Fox, Columbia, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Paramount, RKO, Republic, United Artists, Universal, Walt Disney and Warner Brothers) on the content in the films they would release to the public? How might some of your favorite films and other pop culture installments from the early 20th Century and beyond have gone if all their makers and distributors were given maximum creative freedom within reason to make what they wanted to? Feel free to discuss this entire ATL in the comments.

rubrics.question_focus: What If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had gained First Amendment and union protections much earlier in the twentieth century?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how consistently the response adopts and maintains the specific counterfactual: significantly earlier First Amendment and union protections for U.S. film, comics, and broadcasting in the early twentieth century.
criteria.1-2: Misunderstands or ignores the counterfactual; largely describes actual history.
criteria.3-4: Mentions earlier protections but inconsistently applies them or reverts to real-world constraints (e.g., Hays Code effects unchanged).
criteria.5-6: Applies the premise in parts of the analysis but leaves key institutions or periods unaffected without explanation.
criteria.7-8: Consistently integrates earlier speech and labor protections into most sectors and time periods discussed.
criteria.9-10: Fully re-centers the historical trajectory around early constitutional and union protections, explicitly contrasting with real history and avoiding leakage of actual constraints.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth and Specificity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response explains clear mechanisms linking early protections to changes in content, industry structure, labor relations, regulation, and cultural politics.
criteria.1-2: Offers assertions about outcomes (e.g., 'more creative freedom') with no mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Provides vague causal links (e.g., 'fewer restrictions means edgier content') with minimal elaboration.
criteria.5-6: Explains some mechanisms (e.g., weakened censorship boards, stronger guild bargaining) but leaves others implicit.
criteria.7-8: Details multiple mechanisms across legal, economic, and cultural domains (e.g., court precedents, contract negotiations, market segmentation).
criteria.9-10: Develops interlocking mechanisms (constitutional law → regulatory regimes → studio incentives → genre evolution → audience segmentation → political backlash) with clear step-by-step logic.

criteria.name: Long-Range Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response traces plausible long-term ripple effects across decades rather than focusing only on immediate changes.
criteria.1-2: Discusses only short-term or isolated effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions later consequences but without clear linkage to earlier changes.
criteria.5-6: Outlines a multi-decade trajectory but with gaps or abrupt jumps.
criteria.7-8: Presents a coherent multi-stage evolution from early 20th century to mid/late century outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Constructs a sustained, path-dependent narrative showing how early protections reshape major developments (e.g., censorship regimes, genre cycles, political media battles, labor power) over the century.

criteria.name: Breadth of Downstream Impact Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how comprehensively the response covers major domains affected: content norms, genre development, labor unions, studio/network power, regulatory bodies, audience segmentation, and broader social/political culture.
criteria.1-2: Focuses narrowly on a single medium or effect.
criteria.3-4: Covers two domains (e.g., content and ratings) with limited depth.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several domains but omits significant areas (e.g., labor or broadcasting regulation).
criteria.7-8: Covers most major domains with reasonably balanced attention.
criteria.9-10: Integrates film, comics, and broadcasting with labor, law, market structure, and cultural politics into a unified analysis.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the scenario remains historically and institutionally plausible, acknowledges uncertainty, and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or implausible leaps without justification.
criteria.3-4: Some speculative leaps with little acknowledgment of uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but occasionally overconfident or thinly justified.
criteria.7-8: Maintains plausibility, signals key uncertainties, and avoids contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs alternative pathways, flags contingent factors (e.g., courts, public opinion, economics), and sustains a logically consistent counterfactual throughout.

items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting had gained robust First Amendment protection and strong union protections much earlier in the twentieth century—say in the 1910s or 1920s rather than gradually through mid-century court decisions and labor struggles—the cultural, political, and economic development of American media would likely have looked markedly different.

First, content would probably have been more politically and socially daring much earlier. In reality, film was not fully protected as free speech until *Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson* (1952), and broadcasting remained subject to heavier regulation. Before that, local censorship boards, the Hays Code (from the 1930s), and political pressures constrained what could be depicted. If films and later comics and radio had enjoyed clear First Amendment protections from the outset, self-censorship regimes like the Production Code or the Comics Code Authority might never have emerged, or would have been weaker. Hollywood in the 1920s and 1930s might have addressed racism, labor conflict, sexuality, and class inequality more openly. Comics in the 1940s and 1950s might have developed a broader range of genres—crime, horror, political satire—without the moral panic that led to Senate hearings and industry self-policing. Broadcasting might have aired more controversial political commentary earlier, accelerating the normalization of dissenting voices.

Second, earlier union protections would have reshaped labor relations and industry structure. Stronger, legally protected unions for actors, writers, animators, radio performers, and technical crews in the 1910s or 1920s would likely have curtailed the dominance of vertically integrated studio systems and powerful network executives. Wages and working conditions might have stabilized sooner, reducing exploitation, blacklist practices, and arbitrary contract systems. The Hollywood blacklist of the late 1940s and 1950s, for example, might have been harder to sustain in an environment where speech rights were firmly protected and unions were legally secure. Earlier collective bargaining could also have diversified the workforce over time, especially if unions had pushed for anti-discrimination provisions earlier in the century.

Politically, stronger First Amendment protections for these media might have intensified public debate during key crises such as World War I, the Red Scare, the Great Depression, and World War II. During World War I, the Espionage and Sedition Acts suppressed dissent across media. If courts had already recognized film and broadcasting as core protected speech, government propaganda efforts might have faced greater resistance, and antiwar or socialist perspectives might have remained more visible. This could have normalized a more pluralistic media culture earlier, potentially reducing the sharp oscillations between repression and liberalization that characterized mid-century American politics.

Culturally, earlier protections could have accelerated the breakdown of rigid moral norms. Topics such as interracial relationships, LGBTQ identities, reproductive rights, and critiques of religion might have appeared in mainstream media decades sooner. That said, public backlash might also have intensified. Stronger constitutional protections do not eliminate social pressure; they shift the battleground from legal prohibition to market and political contestation. Boycotts, advertiser pressure, and congressional investigations could still have constrained content, though without the same legal force.

Economically, earlier unionization combined with free speech protections might have reduced the extreme concentration of power in studio moguls and network owners. More independent producers and creators could have entered the market, fostering a more decentralized media ecosystem. On the other hand, higher labor costs and less centralized control might have slowed the rapid industrial expansion that made Hollywood globally dominant in the interwar period. The United States might still have led global entertainment, but perhaps with a more fragmented, less vertically integrated industry.

In sum, earlier First Amendment and union protections for film, comics, and broadcasting would likely have produced a media culture that was more politically open, socially experimental, and labor-secure much earlier in the twentieth century. The United States might have experienced sharper public debates sooner, but also developed a more mature tradition of media pluralism and worker power. The trajectory of American popular culture—and its global influence—would probably have been less morally constrained, less politically repressive, and more structurally balanced between creators and corporate owners.

items.question: What If the Haber process is never invented?
human_answers: there are very very very few inventions that are so dependent on one person or group or situation that they wont get invented without them. Frankly i am not sure i can think of any. Yes it may get delayed but never invented? seams doubtful Now this isn't my area of expertise but. Usually when it is time to railroad you can pretty much count n somene inventing and building a railroad. This is why we often get similar inventions in multiple locations. Even back in the day a lot of inventions that get credited to one country and that other counties then “stole them” probably had more then a few cases of contry B finally get to the same level of knowledge in that area and this leads to someone figuring it out. The differencecis that as we get to more modern times the knowledges of 1st world countries gets closer and closer and spreads thoughout . This is why things like nuclear science, jet engines and radar were all “sort of” being looked at in multiple countries with a relatively short time span. So unless there are some very unusual circumstances odds are someone will eventually figure it out.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.
items.original_question: What if the Haber process is never invented? Let's say that Haber fails to impress Bosch and the BASF in July 1909 due to a failed demonstration of ammonia synthesis. What happens next? Would Haber go elsewhere to find a sponsor, or move on to something else? Cause this would mean that the entire discipline of industrial chemistry is stunted, and high pressure chemistry doesn't exist. Would WW1 even start?

items.model_answer:
If the Haber process had never been invented, the modern world would look dramatically different—economically, demographically, politically, and environmentally. The Haber–Bosch process, developed in the early 20th century, enables the industrial fixation of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which is primarily used to make synthetic fertilizers. Today, roughly half of the nitrogen in human bodies comes from food grown using this process. Without it, global history would have unfolded under much tighter ecological constraints.

Most immediately, global population growth would have been sharply limited. Before synthetic fertilizers, agriculture depended on natural nitrogen sources such as crop rotation, animal manure, compost, and deposits of guano or nitrate minerals. These sources were finite and geographically uneven. By the early 1900s, many regions were already experiencing soil depletion and fears of food shortages. Without industrial nitrogen fixation, agricultural yields would have remained far lower, making it extremely difficult to sustain the 20th century’s population boom. Instead of 8+ billion people today, the global population might have stabilized at perhaps 3–4 billion or even less, depending on technological adaptations and dietary patterns.

This constraint would have reshaped geopolitics. Countries rich in natural nitrate deposits—such as Chile—would have retained enormous strategic importance. Competition for fertilizer resources might have intensified imperial rivalries. During World War I, Germany used the Haber process not only for fertilizer but also to produce explosives from synthetic nitrates after naval blockades cut off access to Chilean saltpeter. Without the process, Germany’s ability to sustain prolonged industrial warfare would have been reduced, potentially shortening the war or altering its outcome. More broadly, industrialized warfare in the 20th century might have been more constrained by limited access to nitrogen-based explosives.

Economic development patterns would also differ. The Green Revolution of the mid-20th century relied heavily on synthetic fertilizers alongside improved crop varieties and irrigation. Without cheap nitrogen fertilizer, many countries in Asia and Latin America might have faced recurring famines or slower development. Urbanization would likely have proceeded more slowly, as fewer agricultural surpluses would be available to support large non-farming populations. Industrialization itself might have been more regionally uneven.

Environmental consequences would be mixed. On one hand, the absence of massive synthetic fertilizer use would mean far less nitrogen runoff, fewer dead zones in oceans, lower nitrous oxide emissions, and reduced groundwater contamination. Biodiversity loss from intensive monoculture farming might have been less severe. On the other hand, to feed growing populations without synthetic fertilizer, societies might have converted even more forests and grasslands into farmland, expanding agricultural land use and accelerating deforestation. The environmental balance would depend on how societies responded—whether by adopting lower-meat diets, stricter population controls, or more sustainable farming methods.

Socially and politically, chronic food scarcity in some regions could have intensified inequality and instability. Governments might have implemented stricter population policies earlier. Migration patterns could have been shaped by soil fertility and access to natural nitrogen sources. Technological innovation might have focused more heavily on biological nitrogen fixation—developing crops with enhanced symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing bacteria—potentially accelerating advances in agricultural biotechnology.

In essence, without the Haber process, humanity would still face the same basic ecological constraint that shaped pre-industrial history: food production limited by naturally available nitrogen. The 20th century’s explosive growth—in population, cities, industrial output, and military capacity—would likely have been tempered. The world might be smaller in population, less industrially intense, and possibly less environmentally nitrogen-polluted—but also more vulnerable to famine and more constrained by the limits of soil fertility.

edus.text: If the Haber process had never been invented, the modern world would look dramatically different—economically, demographically, politically, and environmentally.
The Haber–Bosch process, developed in the early 20th century, enables the industrial fixation of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which is primarily used to make synthetic fertilizers.
Today, roughly half of the nitrogen in human bodies comes from food grown using this process.
Without it, global history would have unfolded under much tighter ecological constraints.
Most immediately, global population growth would have been sharply limited.
Before synthetic fertilizers, agriculture depended on natural nitrogen sources such as crop rotation, animal manure, compost, and deposits of guano or nitrate minerals.
These sources were finite and geographically uneven.
By the early 1900s, many regions were already experiencing soil depletion and fears of food shortages.
Without industrial nitrogen fixation, agricultural yields would have remained far lower, making it extremely difficult to sustain the 20th century’s population boom.
Instead of 8+ billion people today, the global population might have stabilized at perhaps 3–4 billion or even less, depending on technological adaptations and dietary patterns.
This constraint would have reshaped geopolitics.
Countries rich in natural nitrate deposits—such as Chile—would have retained enormous strategic importance.
Competition for fertilizer resources might have intensified imperial rivalries.
During World War I, Germany used the Haber process not only for fertilizer but also to produce explosives from synthetic nitrates after naval blockades cut off access to Chilean saltpeter.
Without the process, Germany’s ability to sustain prolonged industrial warfare would have been reduced, potentially shortening the war or altering its outcome.
More broadly, industrialized warfare in the 20th century might have been more constrained by limited access to nitrogen-based explosives.
Economic development patterns would also differ.
The Green Revolution of the mid-20th century relied heavily on synthetic fertilizers alongside improved crop varieties and irrigation.
Without cheap nitrogen fertilizer, many countries in Asia and Latin America might have faced recurring famines or slower development.
Urbanization would likely have proceeded more slowly, as fewer agricultural surpluses would be available to support large non-farming populations.
Industrialization itself might have been more regionally uneven.
Environmental consequences would be mixed.
On one hand, the absence of massive synthetic fertilizer use would mean far less nitrogen runoff, fewer dead zones in oceans, lower nitrous oxide emissions, and reduced groundwater contamination.
Biodiversity loss from intensive monoculture farming might have been less severe.

On the other hand, to feed growing populations without synthetic fertilizer, societies might have converted even more forests and grasslands into farmland, expanding agricultural land use and accelerating deforestation.
The environmental balance would depend on how societies responded—whether by adopting lower-meat diets, stricter population controls, or more sustainable farming methods.
Socially and politically, chronic food scarcity in some regions could have intensified inequality and instability.
Governments might have implemented stricter population policies earlier.
Migration patterns could have been shaped by soil fertility and access to natural nitrogen sources.

Technological innovation might have focused more heavily on biological nitrogen fixation—developing crops with enhanced symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing bacteria—potentially accelerating advances in agricultural biotechnology.
In essence, without the Haber process, humanity would still face the same basic ecological constraint that shaped pre-industrial history: food production limited by naturally available nitrogen.
The 20th century’s explosive growth—in population, cities, industrial output, and military capacity—would likely have been tempered.

The world might be smaller in population, less industrially intense, and possibly less environmentally nitrogen-polluted—but also more vulnerable to famine and more constrained by the limits of soil fertility.

items.question: "Querfront": What If Strasser split the NSDAP in 1932?
human_answers: Part II: Rise and Fall ​ Theodor Steinhäuser Aufstieg und Fall Hitlers: Eine Geschichte der NSDAP The sudden collapse of the NSDAP in 1933 resulted from many factors, including, but not limited to, the loss of support from the party's industrial backers, the expulsion of many high-ranking members after the formation of the DSU, and President von Hindenburg's reluctance to appoint Hitler as chancellor. Historians agree that the final death blow to the party was the success of the Schleicher-Strasser negotiations in December 1932. After this, many industrial backers grudgingly stopped funding them as it was thought that they had reached their peak already, and started funding prospective Schleicher allies, the DNVP and the DVP, both of which would enter the VDP political alliance in 1933. Roland Schünemann 'Deutscher Sozialismus', Eine Geschichte der Strasseristischen Bewegung Chapter VI: Bildung der DSU The formation of the DSU politically reunited the Strasser brothers, who had been split after Otto Strasser left the NSDAP after he had a confrontation with Joseph Goebbels. Otto Strasser's organization, the Kampfgemeinschaft Revolutionärer Nationalsozialisten, served as a semi-paramilitary organization for the duration of the DSU's existence. The newly-formed DSU granted much parliamentary as well as extraparliamentary support to the von Schleicher cabinet, and was instrumental in the formation of the Zweites Deutsches Kaiserreich. The DSU's program included much of the same as the NSDAP's, however, being more open to entering a coalition as well as being ostensibly anticapitalist, as the Strasser brothers claimed was the original purpose of the NSDAP.
items.original_question: "Querfront": What if Strasser split the NSDAP in 1932? Part I: Secret Dealings ​ December 1932 Reichskanzlei, Wilhelmstraße no. 77, Berlin The night was deep and dark, and a chill was in the air in Berlin. Wilhelmstraße, the street where many of the official German government offices, including the Reichspräsidentenpalais, are located, was especially quiet as the day's normal government activity had concluded. Away from the eye of any onlookers, in a tucked-away office in the Reichskanzlei, the second-most important man in Germany sat. Reichskanzler Kurt von Schleicher smoked a cigar at his desk. His guest was one of the leading figures within the NSDAP, Gregor Strasser, who had only recently arrived to the office. von Schleicher took out his cigar and began talking to Strasser. "Now, you may be wondering why I have called you here," von Schleicher declared. "I would like to offer you a position in my cabinet. Vice-Chancellor, in fact." "What would you like in return, Herr Reichskanzler?" Strasser asked. The general stood up. "Now, you know that my cabinet is only being held up by presidential power. I would like to find a Reichstag majority to support my cabinet, and the support of you and the like-minded Reichstag deputies would be instrumental in providing this. I am prepared to fill the vacancy in the position with you, if you agree to my proposal, however." "I feel accepting this proposal would create the highest ire in Herr Hitler." "Well, you have a large following in the party, correct?" von Schleicher did not wait for Strasser to respond before continuing, "I believe that you could simply split from the party—of course, this new party would join a coalition with some other prospective parties." Strasser quietly asked, "How do you think this would go through easily? The Sturmabteilung is everywhere. How are we supposed to keep it secret during the planning stages?" Now, von Schleicher paused to take a puff of his cigar before continuing, growing more animated as he detailed his plan. "You must keep this very secret, do not share it with anybody! Only you and I must know about this until it is time for the plan to be executed." "And if Hitler finds out?" Schleicher turned to look at Strasser, 10 years his junior, and stared intently into his eyes. "I am sure you would be removed from all political power within the NSDAP. I'm sure you don't want that." Strasser shuddered, perhaps from the cold or the thought of his removal. "I shall consider your offer, Herr Reichskanzler." As Strasser turned to leave, von Schleicher interrupted with one last remark. "Make sure to watch out for anyone who has contacts to Herr Hitler, even indirectly. Do not act suspicious, for they might track you. I shall see you tomorrow." Strasser closed the door, exited the building, and entered the cold winter night.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity (Strasser Split in 1932)
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently and plausibly operationalizes the specific counterfactual that Gregor Strasser successfully splits the NSDAP in 1932, rather than drifting back to actual history.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or contradicts the premise; largely recounts real 1932–1933 events without a genuine split.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a split but inconsistently applies it; major events proceed as in real history without adjustment.
criteria.5-6: Implements the split but with limited detail on timing, scale, or factional consequences.
criteria.7-8: Clearly specifies when and how the split occurs and consistently adjusts subsequent events accordingly.
criteria.9-10: Provides a precise, historically grounded divergence point and rigorously maintains its implications throughout the entire scenario.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth (Political and Institutional Dynamics)
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the response explains the mechanisms linking the NSDAP split to shifts in elites, voters, party financing, Reichstag arithmetic, and presidential decision-making.
criteria.1-2: Relies on assertions (e.g., “Hitler loses power”) without explaining how institutions or actors respond.
criteria.3-4: Offers some causal links but skips key actors (e.g., industrialists, Hindenburg, Reichswehr).
criteria.5-6: Explains several mechanisms but leaves gaps in elite coordination or parliamentary math.
criteria.7-8: Traces detailed interactions among Strasserists, Hitler loyalists, conservatives, and state elites with clear institutional logic.
criteria.9-10: Provides a multi-actor, institutionally grounded causal chain showing how incentives, constraints, and bargaining dynamics reshape outcomes.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects (1933 and Beyond)
criteria.criteria_description: Measures the extent to which the answer develops coherent medium- and long-term consequences beyond the immediate 1932 crisis.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the split or immediate aftermath with no downstream implications.
criteria.3-4: Briefly mentions short-term government changes but no broader regime or geopolitical effects.
criteria.5-6: Covers either domestic regime evolution or foreign policy consequences, but not both in depth.
criteria.7-8: Develops sustained implications for regime type, party system, economic policy, and European geopolitics.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent multi-year trajectory (e.g., constitutional change, authoritarian consolidation or fragmentation, international alignments) with internally consistent ripple effects.

criteria.name: Plausibility and Constraint Awareness (Weimar Context)
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the scenario respects structural constraints of late Weimar Germany, including economic crisis, elite anti-communism, presidential powers, and voter coalitions.
criteria.1-2: Proposes outcomes that ignore basic structural realities (e.g., stable liberal democracy without justification).
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges context but introduces highly speculative leaps without constraint-based reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but underestimates key constraints (e.g., Hindenburg’s preferences or Reichswehr interests).
criteria.7-8: Carefully weighs structural limits and shows how actors work within or around them.
criteria.9-10: Demonstrates nuanced understanding of Weimar political economy and elite calculations, explicitly explaining why the counterfactual remains within realistic bounds.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately signals uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Contains major internal contradictions or presents speculation as certainty.
criteria.3-4: Some inconsistencies or overconfident claims about complex outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but limited acknowledgment of contingency or alternative paths.
criteria.7-8: Logically consistent and explicitly notes key uncertainties or branching possibilities.
criteria.9-10: Maintains full internal coherence while clearly mapping multiple plausible branches and their relative likelihoods without contradiction.

items.model_answer:
If Gregor Strasser had successfully split the NSDAP in 1932, the immediate effect would likely have been to fracture the Nazi movement at its most electorally powerful moment and to weaken Adolf Hitler’s claim to be the indispensable leader of the German nationalist right. Whether that would have prevented Hitler’s rise to the chancellorship depends on how large and durable Strasser’s breakaway faction proved to be, but the consequences could have been significant.

By late 1932 the Nazi Party was already under strain. It had peaked electorally in July 1932 and then lost votes in November. Strasser represented the party’s “left” wing, favoring a more genuinely anti-capitalist, worker-oriented nationalism and showing greater openness to cooperation with trade unions and even elements of the socialist left. If he had formally split—taking with him a meaningful bloc of Reichstag deputies, regional organizers (especially in northern Germany), and SA elements—the NSDAP would have lost its image of unstoppable momentum and internal unity, which was central to Hitler’s appeal to conservative elites.

Such a split might have strengthened Kurt von Schleicher’s efforts to build a “Querfront” (cross-front) coalition. Schleicher hoped to peel off Strasserite Nazis and combine them with trade unionists and moderate conservatives to stabilize the Republic under authoritarian but non-Nazi leadership. If Strasser had broken decisively and brought, say, 20–40 Reichstag deputies and parts of the SA, Schleicher could have presented President Hindenburg with a more viable parliamentary base. This might have prolonged Schleicher’s chancellorship or led to a new authoritarian coalition excluding Hitler.

However, there are limits to how transformative this would have been. Hitler’s personal authority within the NSDAP was immense. Many party members who sympathized with Strasser’s social rhetoric were deeply loyal to Hitler as the movement’s charismatic leader. A split might therefore have reduced the Nazi vote but not destroyed Hitler’s core following. In that case, the right-wing elite—Papen, Hindenburg’s circle, and industrial backers—might still have seen Hitler as the most effective mass leader against the left, even if weakened.

If the split had been large enough, though, it could have denied the Nazis the critical mass that made Hitler appear unavoidable in January 1933. Without a unified Nazi Party commanding the largest bloc in the Reichstag, conservative elites might have continued experimenting with authoritarian presidential cabinets rather than inviting Hitler into power. The fragmentation of the radical right could also have opened space for the Communists and Social Democrats to regain ground, though deep mutual hostility makes a united left response unlikely.

In the longer term, a Strasser-led nationalist-social breakaway might have evolved into a populist, corporatist party competing with both Nazis and traditional conservatives. Germany could still have drifted toward authoritarianism, given the structural weaknesses of Weimar and the Great Depression, but perhaps under a military-conservative regime rather than a totalitarian Nazi one. The specific trajectory toward Hitler’s one-party dictatorship and the particular racial-ideological radicalization that followed might have been averted or at least significantly delayed.

In sum, a successful Strasser split in 1932 would most plausibly have weakened Hitler at a decisive moment and complicated his path to power. It would not automatically have saved the Weimar Republic, but it could have altered the balance among Germany’s authoritarian options—potentially preventing the rapid consolidation of a unified Nazi regime under Hitler in 1933.

By late 1932 the Nazi Party was already under strain.
It had peaked electorally in July 1932 and then lost votes in November.
Strasser represented the party’s “left” wing,
favoring a more genuinely anti-capitalist, worker-oriented nationalism and showing greater openness to cooperation with trade unions and even elements of the socialist left.
If he had formally split—taking with him a meaningful bloc of Reichstag deputies, regional organizers, and SA elements—the NSDAP would have lost its image of unstoppable momentum and internal unity,
which was central to Hitler’s appeal to conservative elites.
Such a split might have strengthened Kurt von Schleicher’s efforts to build a “Querfront” coalition.
Schleicher hoped to peel off Strasserite Nazis and combine them with trade unionists and moderate conservatives to stabilize the Republic under authoritarian but non-Nazi leadership.
If Strasser had broken decisively and brought 20–40 Reichstag deputies and parts of the SA, Schleicher could have presented President Hindenburg with a more viable parliamentary base.
This might have prolonged Schleicher’s chancellorship or led to a new authoritarian coalition excluding Hitler.
However, there are limits to how transformative this would have been.
Hitler’s personal authority within the NSDAP was immense.
Many party members who sympathized with Strasser’s social rhetoric were deeply loyal to Hitler as the movement’s charismatic leader.
A split might therefore have reduced the Nazi vote but not destroyed Hitler’s core following.
In that case, the right-wing elite might still have seen Hitler as the most effective mass leader against the left, even if weakened.
If the split had been large enough, it could have denied the Nazis the critical mass that made Hitler appear unavoidable in January 1933.

Without a unified Nazi Party commanding the largest bloc in the Reichstag, conservative elites might have continued experimenting with authoritarian presidential cabinets rather than inviting Hitler into power.
The fragmentation of the radical right could also have opened space for the Communists and Social Democrats to regain ground,
though deep mutual hostility makes a united left response unlikely.
In the longer term, a Strasser-led nationalist-social breakaway might have evolved into a populist, corporatist party competing with both Nazis and traditional conservatives.
Germany could still have drifted toward authoritarianism, given the structural weaknesses of Weimar and the Great Depression,
but perhaps under a military-conservative regime rather than a totalitarian Nazi one.
The specific trajectory toward Hitler’s one-party dictatorship and the particular racial-ideological radicalization that followed might have been averted or at least significantly delayed.
In sum, a successful Strasser split in 1932 would most plausibly have weakened Hitler at a decisive moment and complicated his path to power.
It would not automatically have saved the Weimar Republic,
but it could have altered the balance among Germany’s authoritarian options—potentially preventing the rapid consolidation of a unified Nazi regime under Hitler in 1933.

items.question: What If the Montreal Expos had remained a Canadian Major League Baseball team?
human_answers: ???????????????????????????????????? Montreal is not a baseball city. It wasn't the Expos' fault that they failed as a MLB team. After Expo 67, IIRC, the establishment of the Montreal "Expos" was seen as an opportunity to capitalize on the Exposition's success. But without fan support, the cavernous emptiness of the Expos' stadium were matched only by its ugliness and increasing dilapidation. In the face of all that, no amount of success on the field was going to keep the Expos north of the border. They were trying to hang on in the 2nd most European city in Canada (after Quebec City), while the Blue Jays enjoyed playing (1) in the most Americanized city in the Great White North (Calgary and Vancouver MIGHT want to argue Toronto's status in that regard, but they probably don't want to). Hell, even Quebec City had a failed NHL franchise. 1) Winning back-to-back World Series championships in 1992-93, with the added layer of Canadian nationalism created in '92 by a poorly displayed Canadian flag by a USMC color guard, helped buck up Toronto's morale enormously.

If the Expos move to Vancouver, it would work best to have them as a natural rival to the Mariners, so moving them to the AL would make a lot of sense. With that in mind, MLB could either move the Rays to DC or put in an expansion team. If they’re not ready to expand, as I suspect they weren’t, say hello to the Washington Nationals as an AL East team, which works fine for the AL as long as everyone is willing to tell the Rangers to eat shit and play their schedule on the West Coast. It means the NL has a choice - see about expanding, ask for a team from the AL to join, send the Marlins to the AL, or just bump the Pirates to the East and go with odd-numbered leagues. They could expand to 32 teams, but that’s a massive headache of its own - having four divisions in each league fucks up the playoffs, and having two divisions in each league means travel headaches (which are solvable but still a pain.) There’s also the question of the A’s and their beshitted stadium, but that one might be more solvable than the Rays and their poorly-attended warehouse.

items.model_answer:
If the Montreal Expos had remained a Canadian Major League Baseball team, the landscape of baseball in Canada—and in parts of the United States—would likely look different in economic, cultural, and competitive terms.

First, Canadian baseball culture would almost certainly be broader and more regionally balanced. Since the Expos relocated to Washington, D.C., in 2005, the Toronto Blue Jays have been Canada’s sole MLB franchise. As a result, they evolved into a de facto national team, drawing fans from coast to coast. If the Expos had stayed, Canada might have developed a sustained two-team rivalry similar to the Yankees–Red Sox dynamic, fostering stronger regional identities between Quebec and Ontario. Montreal’s deep baseball roots—especially its connection to figures like Jackie Robinson and its strong minor league history—could have remained a visible part of MLB’s narrative. A viable Expos franchise might also have strengthened youth development and grassroots baseball in Quebec, where hockey has long dominated.

Second, the economics of MLB would have shifted. The Washington Nationals would not exist in their current form, at least not in Washington. The MLB realignment and revenue flows that followed the Expos’ relocation would have unfolded differently. Montreal’s viability depended heavily on stadium financing and ownership stability. If a new downtown ballpark had been built in the late 1990s or early 2000s, as was proposed, the team might have reversed its attendance decline. With a modern facility and stable ownership, the Expos could have capitalized on the strong teams they fielded in the early 1990s, particularly the 1994 squad that had the best record in baseball before the strike. A competitive, well-financed Expos franchise might have retained star players longer, altering pennant races and even World Series outcomes.

Third, the political and cultural symbolism would matter. Baseball’s presence in Montreal represented not just a sports franchise but a symbolic bridge between francophone Quebec and the broader North American sports market. Retaining the team might have reinforced Montreal’s image as a major-league, cosmopolitan city after a period of economic and demographic uncertainty in the 1990s. It also could have helped MLB expand further into international markets by strengthening its foothold outside the United States, complementing later efforts in Latin America and Asia.

However, this scenario would have required structural changes: improved revenue sharing, a viable stadium deal, and committed local ownership. Without those, the same financial pressures that led to relocation would likely have continued. Even if the Expos had survived, they might have resembled a smaller-market club like Tampa Bay—competitive at times but constrained financially.

In sum, a continued Montreal Expos franchise would likely have deepened Canadian baseball culture, reshaped MLB’s geographic and economic balance, and preserved a distinctive cultural institution in Quebec. The broader structure of Major League Baseball—particularly in Washington, D.C.—would have evolved along a different path, and the symbolic map of the sport in North America would look meaningfully different today.

items.question: What If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset?
human_answers: That would fall under the bad economics heading. Germany and Italy might well have a good aircraft industry but for something of the Tornado's complexity and expense, they would need partners to spread the burden. Germany previously partnered with Fairchild-Hiller-Republic prior to Panavian efforts and as much as I like the G.91, it isn't really in the Tornado's league. In terms of a precedent for an Italian combat twin, the closest I can get is the PD.808GE which was of course originally a joint-venture between Piaggio and Douglas. If a number of nearby industrial/aerospace powerhouse nations have approximately compatible requirements, not to mention nations that you have other economic partnerships with in mind, why on earth wouldn't you consortium-up? Germany would not be so fiscally inept as to squander the opportunity and go it alone. Why would they choose to build an inferior type that their singular budget would necessitate? I know the popular narrative has Germany as the unwilling partner but much like the recent-ish Typhoon discussion, the narrative isn't bone out by the facts. The reality was Germany studied cheaper, less capable alternatives such as single-seat, fixed wing etc. and then ploughed right on with the full capability. Eminently logical and seemingly blown out of proportion by two generations of media. A simple question. If Germany were errmming and ahhhing so, why is it Panavia GmbH ? I realise that this thread is probably designed to engender responses like: RAF F-15Bs! Yeah, man, cool! Fine as far as it goes but not very probable. From my perspective, the premise is more like what if money, industry and defence stop mattering in Europe in the 1970s and my response is

The Marineflieger simply wanted a replacement for the F-104 but that doesn't matter because as OTL showed, whatever the airforce (both branches) wanted it didn't matter because the politicians decided. As an example of this look at the text below: Spoiler: text At least the VAK 191 would fulfill some of the requirements of the Luftwaffe and the Marineflieger. Both coming in single and two-seat variants, fighter/interceptor configuration and nuclear capable strike bomber. Supersonic and subsonic variants. And if the German aerospace industry lobbies enough, they might see one variant put into production as they actually have an existing product that consumed tons of R&D funds and ended up flying. Well, conventional wisdom showed that the single-seat, single-engine, fixed-wing design ended up outliving the variable-geometry twin-engined two-seater one. Yeah I doubt they were happy with their low-level supersonic strike F-104s and F-4s... The VAK 191 could fulfill the low-level supersonic strike-aircraft role.

IIRC the British Taxpayer paid 48% of the R&D cost of the Tornado IDS and I definitely remember that it paid 100% of the ADV's R&D cost. I don't know if HM Treasury could have paid the other 52% of the R&D cost of the IDS and that's the expensive one because it includes the cost of developing the engines and airframe. If that's correct which defence projects have to be cancelled to pay the difference? Then there's the cost of building them. My guess is that the assembly cost of the aircraft would be the same because they were made in three different factories and the same number of RAF aircraft are built in the same factory IOTL and ITTL. The British factory also built all the IDS and ADV that were exported too. However, the economies of scale for the engines, avionics and the "bits" of the airframe will be lost because the number built will be cut from nearly 1,000 to about 550. A lot fewer aircraft to support may put the operating cost up too by increasing the price of spares. Also the British defence industry may not have enough scientists and engineers to do the R&D on its own. Which may mean it takes longer and costs more. Or other defence projects have to be cancelled so the scientists and engineers can be concentrated on the Tornado IDS. OTOH I've heard people say that collaborative projects cost more and take longer than national projects. That's partially because of the extra layer of bureaucracy and mainly for political reasons. Each nation (naturally) wants its share of the work to be the same as the amount as it pays. That produces a less than optimal distribution of the R&D and production contracts. Or at least a worse distribution than a purely national distribution, as national politics means the best firm for the job doesn't necessarily get the contract either. Is there any truth to that? Or is it a false memory?

What if both Germany and Italy for some reason both bail or don't join the PANAVIA Tornado program at it's inception? What are the options regarding this? What does Germany, Italy and the UK do? Could the UK carry on alone? What aircraft could replace the Tornado and fill in this role? Could a two seat, big wing SEPECAT Jaguar work? Would an advanced Buccaneer work with a modern avionics upgrade? Regards

items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset in the late 1960s, the European military aviation landscape would have shifted significantly, both politically and industrially.

First, the Tornado program as it existed would almost certainly have collapsed or been radically redesigned. The aircraft was conceived as a tri-national effort (the UK, West Germany, and Italy) to share development costs for a sophisticated, variable-geometry multirole combat aircraft. The project was expensive and technologically ambitious. Without West Germany and Italy, the United Kingdom would have faced the full financial and technical burden alone. Given the economic pressures Britain faced in the 1970s, it is unlikely London would have pursued the same aircraft independently. The UK might have scaled back requirements, delayed development, or opted to purchase or co-develop an American aircraft such as the F-111 (which Britain had already considered) or later variants of U.S. strike aircraft.

Second, the collapse or downsizing of the program would have weakened European defense industrial cooperation. The Tornado was a cornerstone of multinational aerospace collaboration, helping to establish Airbus-era patterns of joint development and production. Without German and Italian participation, European aerospace integration would have been slower and less institutionalized. The industrial structures that later enabled the Eurofighter Typhoon and other collaborative programs might have emerged later or in a more fragile form.

For West Germany and Italy, withdrawal would likely have pushed them toward U.S. aircraft purchases to meet NATO commitments. West Germany, in particular, needed a modern strike aircraft for its central front role in NATO. A direct purchase of advanced American aircraft would have deepened transatlantic defense ties but reduced domestic aerospace development in those countries. Their aerospace industries—especially Germany’s—would have lost valuable experience in complex systems integration and multinational production management.

Strategically within NATO, reliance on U.S. platforms would have increased standardization but also reinforced European dependence on American defense technology. Politically, this might have reduced European leverage in alliance planning and procurement. The symbolic value of Europe demonstrating it could jointly produce a cutting-edge combat aircraft would have been lost.

Finally, the absence of the Tornado as a shared European success might have made later collaboration, including the Eurofighter program, more difficult. Trust, institutional habits, and industrial interdependence built through Tornado were critical foundations. Without them, Europe’s path toward a semi-autonomous defense industrial base would likely have been slower and more fragmented.

In short, West German and Italian withdrawal at the outset would probably have ended the Tornado as a trilateral project, increased European reliance on U.S. aircraft, weakened early European aerospace integration, and delayed the evolution of cooperative defense programs that became central to Europe’s later strategic autonomy efforts.

edus.text: If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset in the late 1960s, the European military aviation landscape would have shifted significantly, both politically and industrially.
First, the Tornado program as it existed would almost certainly have collapsed or been radically redesigned.
The aircraft was conceived as a tri-national effort (the UK, West Germany, and Italy) to share development costs for a sophisticated, variable-geometry multirole combat aircraft.
The project was expensive and technologically ambitious.
Without West Germany and Italy, the United Kingdom would have faced the full financial and technical burden alone.
Given the economic pressures Britain faced in the 1970s, it is unlikely London would have pursued the same aircraft independently.

The UK might have scaled back requirements, delayed development, or opted to purchase or co-develop an American aircraft such as the F-111 (which Britain had already considered) or later variants of U.S. strike aircraft.
Second, the collapse or downsizing of the program would have weakened European defense industrial cooperation.
The Tornado was a cornerstone of multinational aerospace collaboration, helping to establish Airbus-era patterns of joint development and production.
Without German and Italian participation, European aerospace integration would have been slower and less institutionalized.
The industrial structures that later enabled the Eurofighter Typhoon and other collaborative programs might have emerged later or in a more fragile form.
For West Germany and Italy, withdrawal would likely have pushed them toward U.S. aircraft purchases to meet NATO commitments.
West Germany, in particular, needed a modern strike aircraft for its central front role in NATO.
A direct purchase of advanced American aircraft would have deepened transatlantic defense ties but reduced domestic aerospace development in those countries.
Their aerospace industries—especially Germany’s—would have lost valuable experience in complex systems integration and multinational production management.
Strategically within NATO, reliance on U.S. platforms would have increased standardization but also reinforced European dependence on American defense technology.
Politically, this might have reduced European leverage in alliance planning and procurement.
The symbolic value of Europe demonstrating it could jointly produce a cutting-edge combat aircraft would have been lost.
Finally, the absence of the Tornado as a shared European success might have made later collaboration, including the Eurofighter program, more difficult.
Trust, institutional habits, and industrial interdependence built through Tornado were critical foundations.
Without them, Europe’s path toward a semi-autonomous defense industrial base would likely have been slower and more fragmented.

In short, West German and Italian withdrawal at the outset would probably have ended the Tornado as a trilateral project, increased European reliance on U.S. aircraft, weakened early European aerospace integration, and delayed the evolution of cooperative defense programs that became central to Europe’s later strategic autonomy efforts.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. Physics simply allows for them so once you get the combination of the understanding of physics and the industrial/technical ability to make them you are getting them. And it is not exactly all that high tech to build a gun type nuke. So I just don’t see how you delay the development all that long. You would need the U.S. and the USSR to both come out of WW2 in much much worse shape to the point that they simply can’t afford to build nukes and I don’t see that happening.
items.original_question: What if No nuclear weapons? No Tubes Alloy or Los Alamos, and no German atomic research. Sadly, Japan is invaded - high causalities on both sides especially Japanese civilians much of it from starvation. No organised surrender, just quiet acceptance from district, to town, then the next. Japanese Americans were 'encouraged' to return to the homeland and rebuild - from the stone age! But what happens - with no nuclear umbrella - no ballistic missiles. WMD were confined to the Grandslams & Tallboys, with fuel air explosives via aircraft bombs or short range (V2) missiles. Research was more focused on better guidance for V1 type cruise missiles, and other ASM. Would the Berlin Blockade still happen, would it get hot? How would this affect Defence spending? Where would the focus on the difference between here and OTL?

items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never been developed, the political, military, and moral landscape of the modern world would look very different—but not necessarily more peaceful.

The most immediate difference would be the absence of nuclear deterrence. During the Cold War, the doctrine of mutually assured destruction (MAD) discouraged the United States and the Soviet Union from engaging in direct large-scale war. Without nuclear weapons, it is plausible that conflicts such as the Berlin crises or the Cuban Missile Crisis could have escalated into full conventional wars between superpowers. A third world war might have been more likely, fought with conventional forces on a massive scale across Europe or Asia, potentially causing enormous casualties even without nuclear devastation.

On the other hand, the existential threat posed by nuclear annihilation would not have shaped global politics. Much of the intense arms racing, civil defense planning, and diplomatic tension of the Cold War revolved around nuclear arsenals. Without them, military competition would likely have focused more heavily on conventional weapons, chemical and biological weapons, or advanced technologies such as cyber and space-based systems. Some of these alternatives could also have produced catastrophic consequences, though likely more regionally confined than global nuclear war.

The moral and psychological impact would also differ. Nuclear weapons created a unique sense of shared human vulnerability—the understanding that civilization itself could be destroyed in hours. This fear contributed to global nonproliferation treaties, peace movements, and international cooperation efforts. Without nuclear weapons, there might have been less urgency behind arms control regimes and fewer incentives for major powers to maintain strategic stability.

Geopolitically, some smaller states might have felt more secure without the shadow of nuclear coercion, while others might have felt less secure without nuclear umbrellas provided by allies. Countries like Japan or South Korea, for example, rely partly on extended nuclear deterrence from the United States. In a non-nuclear world, alliances and military doctrines would have evolved differently, possibly with larger standing conventional armies.

In short, a world without nuclear weapons might have avoided the risk of global annihilation and the moral horror associated with Hiroshima and Nagasaki. However, it would not necessarily have been a peaceful world. Great power rivalry, technological arms races, and large-scale wars could still have occurred—perhaps more frequently, though less apocalyptically. Nuclear weapons did not eliminate conflict, but they reshaped it in profound and paradoxical ways.
